I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time

issues.explanation: The profile omits both Triggers and Threat entirely, yet includes carrying a weapon and persistent on-guard appraisals. For a 60-year-old male with military trauma, these items are individually plausible, but together they imply an active current-danger/threat system that is not represented elsewhere in the selected nodes and sits poorly with the formulation, where Threat and Triggers are not linked to the active network.

issues.item: Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time
issues.explanation: 'I have to be on guard all the time' functions more like a live threat appraisal, but the formulation centers the case on a Negative Appraisals ↔ Memory ↔ Maladaptive Strategies loop, with Threat inactive. In the absence of any other threat-focused items, this item is the main source of incoherence.

issues.item: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
issues.explanation: 'Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning' implies salient cue-driven triggering, but all Triggers edges are inactive and no Trigger items are selected. That does not by itself make triggered recall impossible, but combined with the otherwise appraisal/guilt/identity-focused formulation and profile, it is the least coherent memory item.

issues.item: Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
issues.explanation: This item is difficult to reconcile with the formulation because Threat is not otherwise represented in the self-report and all Threat-related edges are inactive. The rest of the profile is organized around guilt/identity loss and trauma memory, whereas constant threat scanning implies an active current-threat focus that is not supported by the selected Threat, Trigger, Appraisal, or Memory items. The avoidance items fit the military trauma context, but this hypervigilant checking behavior appears clinically disconnected from the rest of the profile.

vignette:
Frank is a sixty-year-old warehouse worker who lives with his partner in a mid-sized Midwestern town. He came to therapy at his partner's urging, though he was not sure what talking could do now. What he carried with him was a single night in Vietnam, fifty years ago, that had never stopped happening. He had been a young infantryman, barely nineteen, when his unit was ambushed in a rice paddy at dusk. He remembered the wet heat, the shouting, the way the mud sucked at his boots. He remembered a friend-a boy from Ohio named Danny-taking a round to the chest right next to him. Frank had tried to drag him to cover, but Danny was already gone. He remembered the medevac coming in, the rotors whipping the smoke, and how he had been the one lifted onto the bird while three others were left behind. He had not chosen to be first. He had not even understood what was happening until he was already in the air, watching the paddy shrink beneath him. But that did not matter. What mattered was that he got out and they did not.

For decades, Frank had managed. He worked, he drank, he kept his head down. But in the last few years, the memories had become harder to push away. When they came, they came with the same terror he had felt at nineteen-his chest would seize, his palms would sweat, and he would be back in that paddy, the smell of mud and diesel in his nostrils. And alongside the terror came a guilt so heavy it felt physical. He would see Danny's face, hear his own voice screaming for help, and he would think: Why him and not me? He had no answer. He had never found one. And that absence of an answer had become a kind of answer in itself-that he was not meant to have survived, that his life since had been borrowed time, that the man who came home was not really the same person. He did not know himself anymore. The world, which had once seemed ordinary, now felt like a place where danger could spring from anywhere, at any moment, without warning. He found himself scanning parking lots, watching doorways, noticing the way people moved. He was always ready for something to go wrong.

Frank worked the night shift at a regional distribution center, unloading pallets and stacking boxes. The work was physical and mindless, which suited him. But the warehouse itself had become a problem. It was a low, concrete building with fluorescent lights that buzzed and flickered, and the loading bay doors opened onto a dark yard that reminded him, in some way he could not articulate, of the edge of that rice paddy. He had started taking routes through the building that kept him away from the bay doors. He avoided the break room because someone had left a jacket on a hook that looked too much like an old fatigue shirt. He had stopped wearing olive green or khaki entirely, even though those colors had been staples of his wardrobe for years. He wore only black or navy now. At home, he kept the television on constantly-sports, news, anything-because silence made his mind drift toward the event, and he had learned that if he let himself think about it, he would be stuck there for hours, unable to find the words to describe what he saw or felt. He would open his mouth and nothing would come out. So he did not try.

The consequences of these strategies had been slow but real. His partner had noticed that he no longer went to the grocery store that sat near the old VFW hall, even though it was the closest one. He claimed it was out of the way, but she knew better. He had stopped attending family barbecues at a cousin's house that was located on a street that reminded him, distantly, of the road leading to the deployment base. His social world had shrunk to work and home, and even home had become tense. His partner had tried to get him to talk, but he could not. The words were not there. And so she had finally made the appointment for him, and he had agreed because he was tired-tired of the scanning, the avoiding, the guilt that sat on his chest like a weight he could not set down.

What Frank hoped for, when he walked into the therapist's office, was unclear to him. He did not expect to feel better. He did not expect to forgive himself. But he was afraid that if he did not try something, he would lose the one person who still looked at him like he was worth saving. And that, more than anything else, was what finally brought him through the door.
